title: The Extinct Tasmanian Tiger’s Bite Was Unlike Any Other Predatory Mammal’s - Nautilus
gist: A new bite-force study of the extinct thylacine (Tasmanian tiger) suggests the animal likely never posed a real threat to livestock, undercutting the historical justification used for the bounty campaign that drove it to extinction.

themes.theme: Extinction driven by a mistaken threat narrative

insights.claim: An estimated 3,500 thylacines were killed under bounty programs established by farmers and later the Tasmanian government in the early 19th century, aimed at protecting cattle and sheep, with conservation efforts arriving only weeks before the last known thylacine died in captivity.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A precise, sourced extinction-driver data point (bounty-driven overkill) that quantifies how quickly a targeted eradication campaign can eliminate a species when backed by government incentives.

insights.claim: A new study analyzing the thylacine's bite mechanics indicates the animal likely never had the bite strength needed to pose a real threat to livestock, contradicting the premise that justified the bounty-driven extermination campaign.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A textbook case of a species driven extinct based on an empirically false threat narrative — a cautionary historical precedent relevant to current debates over predator-control policy and livestock-protection lobbying.
